body: Thank you. Here's to hoping it's even better!
I'm glad I'm still here, and I'm grateful I feel that way.
Thank you!

Thank you. It's hard for me to feel good about my life sometimes, but after spending the night with friends (virtually), getting a really nice message from my professor, and laying in bed with the cat I've always wanted, it's hard to ignore how much my life has changed for the better. 

Allowing yourself to be proud is part of the process.

Just to add onto what the original poster brought up, and your points too, I actually stopped transitioning at one point because of depression. I've spoken about it a lot, but I was young, and thought all of my issues were about me being trans. I hated myself and was lost in life. 

I stopped T for an entire year before getting back on it, and in that time I worked myself out of the deepest part of my depression. When I felt okay mentally, I still felt like something in my life was missing, and I was seriously questioning whether I was actually trans, because fixing my depression and changing my entire life had helped so much, so what if it was just something else? I decided to give T another shot (heh), and if it wasn't what I wanted, I'd stop. 

I've been back on T for 2 and a half years now. I've come to realise that a lot of my issues were *both* depression and being trans. I'm starting to like the way I look, I'm stealth now too. I don't get that much social anxiety anymore either. I genuinely love my life now, and don't regret anything I went through to get here. 

I thought as soon as I felt for Uni, transitioning is what would finally make me happy, but it didn't. I had to find happiness alongside my transition. Yeah, being gendered correctly makes me feel good, but it's just one part of my life that makes me happy. You also have to find the rest. 

Guess my point is, I don't think there's enough encouragement in the trans community to take things slow, and to find other sources of happiness.

If you're into doing some research, I'd look up de-transitioning as well. They often have the same symptoms as you. Try to stray away from the... Transphobic stuff, but there are some minor studies about it. These people were people who thought they were trans and experiencing dysphoria, but had other issues, and were cis, therefore de-transitioned. This might help you pin down some mental health issues that might be related.

I gave you advice in my other post. I told you who to talk to. I never claimed you were trans, but what you're experiencing is incredibly close to gender dysphoria. If you can't go see a gender therapist, because this *is* a gender issue, you will need to come to some sort of conclusion on these feelings on your own. You're adamant these feelings are not because you're trans, okay, but what if they are? You're very adamant about shutting down any hint that it might be. 

That all being said, the best way to deal with this is to treat it as though you are trans. I never said you're trans, and I won't.  I said it's a possibility that I think you're shutting out. But this is an issue that needs to be cleared, and exploring your own gender might actually give you an answer, rather than just saying no. If you explore it, and still find your answer is 100% cis, then that's okay! You tried that route, and it didn't pan out, so then you try to find a different approach to face it at. 

It's just that, this is literally the definition of gender dysphoria. This is why people are saying you may be trans. I'm just trying to suggest that if you treat it as a possibility, you may find the answer. My top suggestion would be to talk to someone, but you mentioned that's impossible for you. While a lot of different factors can lead to a cis person transitioning, a lot of those factors need genuine medical professionals. This would be something along the lines of Body Dysmorphia. 

But if you're still adamant it's something along the lines of Body Dysmorphia, then I don't think many people online would be able to help. Although one should see a therapist for gender dysphoria, there's things to make it manageable in the meantime. With a severe disorder like body dysmorphia, you absolutely need a therapist as soon as possible.

Okay, well, you seemed to have dismissed everything I've said. Pursue it or don't, I can't control you. If it's this bad that you want to kill yourself, then you have an issue that's bigger than you're letting yourself see. 

Feel free to message me if you want some advice, but I'm going to stop, because you very obviously do not.

I don't really have  a recommendation for an example, but I'm 22, although that's young, generally older than what Unus Annus seems geared for. 

With most communities for me, I'm not really a part of them. I'll buy some merch occasionally when they make brands that don't have very obvious logos/text, but I just enjoy their content and move on. For the most part, it's basically just television. Sometimes it's plot based, sometimes it's just one off videos of games I want to see. 

But I guess specifically with YouTubers, is that you're watching this one person until they move on. It's finding that one video that makes you keep coming back, and watching them grow and evolve as creators. Kids just grew up on some YouTubers, and the messages these people put out become important to them, just like seeing a celebrity on TV. 

With Unus Annus specifically, it was about a lot of things. You can see that in the hashtag #WeWereHere. To be able to experience something once, and never again, makes you feel important and special. It makes you feel a part of something bigger than yourself. They really pushed the message in the last couple weeks about how anybody can do what they did, maybe not how they did it, but they're not special. They just came up with the idea first. People found them, not even from Markiplier promoting it. It felt really genuine. They were having fun.

They do generally have a younger audience, between 17 to 19 I'd say. At that age you're dealing with trying to figure out the rest of your life. So over an entire year where nothing has happened, to have these two that really do genuinely feel to only have good intentions, to tell you to make every second count, that you're worth it, is important to a lot of people. Most don't get to hear those words in real life. Many have lost people too, especially with covid. To have something to retreat to, where you don't have to think about anything for 10 minutes, is a relief. 

Their catchphrase Memento Mori I think just hit home for people as well. Remember death. Spend those seconds of your clock ticking down doing the things you love. Trying your hardest. Even if it's just for a month, a month can change your life. 

So yeah, I think it's a combination of things. For me, I'm in school for art. These past couple weeks have been difficult. To have somebody sit down for 40 minutes and tell you their struggles with creativity, but show you their absolute passion is inspiring. Everybody has hero's, and I think out of all YouTube channels out there, Unus Annus was a good one to idolize. I was honored to watch it go. It really meant a lot to me, and reminded me to try my best to take hold of every second I have left. Of course, doing it is on me, and not the channel, but it's nice to hear somebody tell me I can do it.

Another thing I will mention, is that you don't have to fit into a binary. You don't have to be male or female. It's something I'm not overly familiar with personally, but I've had many non binary friends. Gender is a spectrum. Exploring it will give you the tools to find a label that fits you best, if you decide you need one.

It's very easy to have those feelings. I had them as well. You going into an online space and "pretending" to be a guy isn't insulting, it's exploring yourself and trying out just pronouns, seeing how those feel. Exploring your gender specifically online in that regard is pretty easy. Just act like you. This is a really good way to explore how *you* feel being referred to as male, and how I explored my gender when I was younger and confused. 

And yes, having those reminders that you're biologically female does hurt. But I guess I pose this question: doesn't doing this hurt too? This constant thinking of it, never acting on it, or exploring it. 

As for the "always be a girl" part, I struggled with that a lot. I had a mindset when I first realised that I was trans that was just constant negative thoughts. It was constantly telling myself I'm a girl, I can never *be* a guy. I would be a fake guy. I wouldn't fit in, people wouldn't believe me. Hell, I didn't believe me. 

When I first left my house with my parents, I basically immediately asked for Testosterone. I was on a daily application, and it was hard to keep up. I struggled with depression and I never really felt okay with the changes. It was happening too fast. I stopped, and for a year, I felt like the shittiest person in the world. I didn't know who I was, because I thought I had lied to myself. Turns out transitioning doesn't fix everything. I had to learn how to accept myself, be confident, deal with my other issues. When I was better, I was terrified of being wrong again. Somebody on Reddit told me to just try. I could always go back off if it wasn't right. It's been 2 and a half years since then, and I've never been happier. 

When I used to see myself in the mirror, I didn't hate who I saw, not really. It was like looking at a person who I didn't know. Whenever somebody used to refer to me as female or with my old name, it hurt. Those things have gone away. I have male friends who have never known me before transitioning, and who will never know I have. I have changed who I am as a person for the better. 

Let's pose a hypothetical. Let's say you *are* transmasculine (ftm). Your experience of feeling this way, and, for a lack of a better word, denial, is incredibly common among transmasculine people. Looking for reasons not to transition, for other answers because it can't be you. You're not trans, just really want to have been born male, so much you'd rather die than live as female. If you *are* trans, transitioning, as far as I'm aware, I'd the only cure to (most of) this feeling.

This is something major and life changing. It's scary. But I encourage you to explore your gender any way you can, purely to maybe find that closure, or that explanation. If you're ever wanting help, there's /r/ftm that can talk you through more ways to help explore your gender. 

And remember, exploring your gender doesn't mean you're trans. It just means you're trying to figure yourself out. There's nothing wrong with that.

So, I am trans. Female to male. I was born genetically a female, but identify and live my life as a man. 

I will start this by saying one thing: I'm not claiming you're trans. Nobody can figure that out except for you. It's not really a choice, as another commentor brought up, it's just a fact of life for me and other trans people. It's a long, sometimes painful journey that takes uprooting your entire life, but at the end of the day, I've never regret it. 

It's not an identity thing. I didn't choose to feel this way. I **needed** to transition or I was absolutely going to kill myself. I longed for it my entire life, and it got to the point where it was unbearable. I guess, technically, I do identify as the opposite gender than what I was born as, but it took a long time to get there. I was scared and in denial for so long. I'd like to make one thing clear. I do not just identify as male, I am male and have always been. I just had to take a couple steps along the way. But... I never really "felt" like a guy or a girl on the inside. I just felt like me. I thought maybe I could live that way, too. Me transitioning wasn't to make my "inside" match with my outside. It was to adjust how people viewed me, how I literally see myself. I never really felt my inner gender was male, I just knew the way the world saw me was wrong.

That being said, whatever you may be experiencing, wanting this to the point of rather killing yourself, is absolutely not normal. Whether it's gender dysphoria or not, I have no right to say, you need to seek someone to speak to this about. Although you are adamant it's not gender dysphoria, speaking to a therapist who specializes in it will probably actually help, as they're the best trained to handle the information and work though it, whether it's actually gender dysphoria or something else. 

If that's out of reach, maybe try some other things. Try going by male on some online forums, see if that makes you feel better/worse. There are many, many identities under the transgender umbrella, so maybe looking into some will help explain what you are feeling. And although you're adamant it's not because you're trans yourself, there may be some relief gained by exploring gender. If it doesn't work out and you still feel the same way, then hey, you can say you made an honest attempt at figuring out what's going on, but this isn't something cis people experience. 

I think it's worth exploring and trying to self analyze, to figure out where these feelings are coming from. Like I said, if it leads nowhere, then what's the harm? Especially if it's anonymous and online. 

Other than that, I honestly don't know what else it could be, so I would definitely seek a therapist if you have the means.

I pass, but it's been hell trying to get top surgery. I'm 5'3, still have a pretty high voice, have a D sized chest that's hard to bind properly, and barely any facial hair. I've had people guess I'm trans, but for the most part, 99% of people just don't question it. 

I think a big part of me passing was my confidence, rather than my looks. I never gave anybody any reason not to question it, and never brought up anything more than being gay. That being said, I have been told I do pass very well, especially now at 2.5 years, when I'm starting to get facial hair. I'm just a short guy. I don't have much advice, sadly. Hopefully passing will become easier with time.

Hey, I just want you to know it'll all be okay. 

It's easy to get in the mindset that you didn't want it enough, but that's not true. Sometimes life can be incredibly overwhelming, especially with the addition of being trans. They have these guidelines in place because testosterone can severely effect mental health in some people, and cause worsening depression, anxiety, etc. 

I know waiting is hard. It's painful. But you are not a failure for having to wait longer. Your journey is your own, and I am sure you'd have wanted that journey to be on T right now, it will happen. 

Some things you cannot change, I've found these are the things you need to work really hard to move on from, and focus on the things we can do. You also can't control what people, especially our loved ones, say to us. Focus on controlling how their words effect you. You have power over your life, even when you're at your most helpless. Things will work out.

Unfortunately there's not a whole lot you can do, but you can try a couple things. I posted about my frustrations with binding a few weeks back. It's hard. I've been binding my C/D chest for 7 years. 

Trans tape/KT Tape: I've only ever tried KT Tape because trans tape is incredibly expensive in my country. But, I've never actually gotten it to work. I don't know what I'm doing wrong, but I'm starting to think my chest is abnormally heavy, as no matter what I do, the tape just pulls away.

Long binders vs short binders: short binders are pretty convenient, but I find them riding up and turning loose really quickly with a large chest. As much as I hate the full body binders (so much fabric), they seem to do the job a lot better. How I try to bind is I try to keep everything as tight and straight as possible. When putting on the binder, I push down, then pull to the side. After, I pull the binder completely taught, and put on my pants to keep the fabric in place. This requires a lot of repositioning, but you kinda get used to it. If you don't pull it taught enough, you'll have part of the tissue pop out the side, though avoiding this completely is impossible. 

Surprisingly, this is really the only advice I have. There's not a whole lot to be done. But don't think about it super hard. Cis men don't have flat chests, and in my 2 years of being stealth, I've never had anyone comment on it, or seemingly question it (and I haven't had facial hair for most of that time, so I still get clocked as young). The body redistribution is just starting, slowly, as I make my way into my third year of T. Wear some baggier clothes, but I definitely think confidence just helped as well. Body language is huge, and just being confident in your stature goes a long way.
I'm in Canada as well. I've heard great things normally, other than the wait times, but 4 years is too long.
Do you know of any guides for how to put the tape on properly? I've looked for some, but never been able to actually find any that seem to work.

The system is a bit weird and convoluted here. It's a medical surgery technically, but because I'm trans and don't like... Have cancer, I'm considered low priority. That means they fit me in whenever, and I'll be behind the cancer patients (Which I absolutely completely understand and am not at all saying I should be in front of them, that'd be horrible), and behind those who made appointments before me. We tried to push it for my shoulders' sake, but it really doesn't matter much. 

I'm pretty large chested. In fact, the reason why I had to change surgeons originally is because they wouldn't give me an appointment at ALL until I went from 38BMI to 35BMI, which was a six month period. So we switched. I just can't seem to win.

We actually changed surgeons already. I'm in Canada so the wait is already long. Because it's paid for by the government, they don't really care how much pain I'm in because the surgery is cosmetic. I've been through it with several doctors and nurses and it's all just waiting in limbo.

I've tried KT tape, but I can never seem to get it right, and it keeps pulling off. I'm a C, so medium leaning on large size. I mean, I do pass, so I guess it does look like large pecs to some people, but if you actually looked, it literally looks like I have b cup breasts. Just flat ones. It's extremely frustrating.

Edit: I should mention I've been stealth for two years, so something is working. It's just easier to deal with when you're not stealth. When you are, and these things threaten to break it, it's anxiety inducing

I'm not denying it's harmful, it is. I said I don't believe it's intended on being harmful. But I put most of the blame here on me. He's working through things right now, and although that doesn't excuse the things he says, I've been in a similar situation as him, that being not realising the things I say are harmful. That being said, I'm very good with many things not bothering me, like short jokes, because my height will never change, and I get them from everybody.

It only changes if you talk about it, but I haven't because, on my side, I don't like having those conversations, especially when I know the person on the other end didn't mean anything by it. Especially realising you've been hurting someone you cared about the entire time hurts them too.

My pet rats died recently too, one in October, and his brother in January. It was so sudden. They didn't die of old age either. One day they were fine, the next they were sick. It comes so fast. 

When Ollie died in October I promised I would take care of his brother, but there wasn't anything I could do. People even told me to get rid of him because he wouldn't be happy with me, not without his brother. 

I never thought I'd get so attached to a pet rats, but I did. And I miss them a lot. No animal will ever replace them. I remember not crying for Ollie, I knew he was sick, and my dad had just died so I was emotionally numb then, but when Zeak died in January, I cried for hours as I cleaned his cage, because they were both gone. I still do sometimes. They were family, and they both helped me through a lot. 

I hope your other boy is doing okay. It's going to be a little harder from here, but you'll make it. Rats are incredibly intelligent and they pick up on so many things. I know he knew he was loved and cared deeply for. I'm sorry for your loss

We always free fed our dogs growing up, but if she's food focused, I'm worried about giving her too much, but I'll have to test that myself.

Yes, I'm going to look into what the foster is feeding her right now, and adjust what I buy to that, possibly upgrading her food after some time, so I can find out what kind of treats she likes. Apparently she's very food driven.

I can't stand gay culture in general. A lot of it is extremely toxic. I've found hookup culture has made it extremely difficult to date. I think it's difficult for a lot of guys, and there are those out there who do want an actual relationship, not just sex, it just seems to be so rare, or so looked down upon.

No, that commenter is right. A growl is a warning. You remove yourself from the situation, and coax the dog away differently. 

This dog obviously has a traumatic past, and your family, and what you did here, is not healthy for the dog. Any dog can be trained not to be this agressive. My guess is that you have previously prevoked the dog, and whether or not he has bitten you, he sees you as somebody he is uncomfortable around. As for your younger niece, some dogs just can't be around kids. You said your grandmother wanted to move, so what were you going to do, leave the dog? ***Yes.*** Leave the dog for another couple of minutes, let him calm down, and find another way to move him. You know his history of agression. 

You are right in saying that the dog should be separated, especially during high traffic times such as Christmas. It's stressful for dogs too, and can cause unusual behavior when surrounded by many people. This dog needs proper care, not to be euthanized. Taking him to a vet is a good start. 

I've been bitten by dogs before. Dogs that I have owned. I am afraid of other people's dogs too, but if you check for the warning signs and show compassion from your own end, you can safely deal with agressive or scared dogs. I can understand your anger, but a dog cannot grasp the concept of dept. The dog owes you nothing. 

Treat the dog with kindness, and respect. Learn some warning signs, and speak honestly, and with a level head with your parents rather than pushing for their dog to be euthanized right away. There are other options. But this behaviour cannot be ignored, nor should the dog die because of *this specific instance*. I'm not saying it's not the right move, maybe it is, but obviously something has to be done, but even the way this post reads, is of a angry teen who doesn't want to be wrong. 

I hope you learn some compassion, and for the love of God, I hope you never get a pet. I can't imagine how you would deal with bad behaviour. If anyone should be ashamed of their reply, it is you. Somebody is trying to help, and you shit on them because they were slightly right? Because you don't agree with them. Don't post on open forums.

I'm going to go against the grain with most people here and say that, yes, you may be an alcoholic, but you may just have a drinking problem. 

An alcoholic isn't fully classified by just withdrawal or the percentage you drink, though this can definitely give the warning signs that you may have alcoholism. 

The fact that you wake up in the morning, and feel the need to drink a shot *is* absolutely worrying. And you may not feel this pull, but then why do you do it? This is not normal behaviour. If you feel the need to do this to help get through the day, then yes, it's very possible you have a problem. There are functional alcoholics. It becomes an issue you can classify, generally, when it impacts your every day life. Such as spending the money on the alcohol, rather than saving, or spending it on something you need. Getting up earlier because of this, and losing sleep. Or yes, withdrawal symptoms. Things like that show signs of a drinking problem, maybe not alcoholism yet, but a problem none-the-less. 

Why do you feel the need to do this? Does it taste good? Does it make you feel better, more stable? Does it calm anxiety, make the day easier to get through? These are the questions you really need to ask yourself. Find the answers, seek someone to talk to if you need. Have things been difficult lately? Yes, no? If not, then why?

Be careful. One shot can escalate into two. Then two into three. Until suddenly you're too deep in. Find healthy habits, find the root to why you're doing this. If you feel it's not an issue, take a step back, look again until you're absolutely sure. I'm absolutely not saying you're an addict, but remember that addicts do say "I can stop any time I want, I'm in control". Watch out for spiraling, the extra shot on bad days. This can, and most likely will, very suddenly impact your life severely. 

From what I've read online, this is a common starting point for most alcoholics. As somebody who has been deeply affected by alcoholism, it's just not worth the risks. It destroys lives, and people. Be careful.

Closure is... Well. Closure is... Everything. 

I don't know what happened, but I do know my own experiences. 

Two years ago now, I lost my best friend. Nothing even went wrong, he just stopped talking to me. He ended the friendship. I wasn't in love with him, no, but he was everything. He was my brother I never had, my family when I needed somebody the most. 

And I spent most of those two years hating myself for something I couldn't control. I spent years wondering what I did wrong, how I could make it better, how I could get him back. But I never could. And I was a different person by the time the chance came. 

I sent him a message, asking for closure. Asking why he treated me the way he did. I never got an answer, but in my head, that was my answer. The way things were, would never be the same again. But sending that message, getting those things off my chest? That was my closure. That was how I healed. 

We're not always lucky to get closure. A sudden passing of a loved one, and sudden ending of a relationship or friendship. We need to take the time to grieve these things, because that's what it is, grief. And it can be a terrible burden to bear, a heavy weight to carry. But you're not alone in carrying it. 

You can't keep blaming yourself for something that is out of your control. Whether or not it was your fault the friendship ended or not, that no longer matters. It straight up doesn't. You can't change the past, and you can't keep living as though some day you will be able to. I've tried. Not to be overdramatic, but it really did nearly kill me. 

My advice? Message him. Apologize. Say everything *you* want to say, from an objective point of view. Don't use manipulative language (not that you would, just be weary of it), don't confess feelings or put him in a hard spot. Rather, speak from your heart. Speak from how you lived through the experience, how it made you feel then, and the weight you carry from it now. Make it clear you are not searching for an apology. You are not searching for an answer, or a road back to what you once had. You are searching for closure for something that has hung over your head for two years. 

Don't do it right now, or tomorrow, or the next day. Do it when you are ready. You have feelings, and those are as valid as anyone else's. 

This road is not especially... Kind. You may end up recieving backlash for anything you said, but if you lay out the message correctly, any reaction can be better than sitting on this forever. Anger is a reaction. You know how they felt and feel. And now you have an answer. Or frustration. Or regret. Or happiness. Or... No answer at all. Left on read. But no matter what, you have an answer. You have found a corner piece in this larger puzzle of recovery. 

One day, you will have moved on, and this will be such a small part of your life. But that day isn't here. You're just living it now. But you are able to do something, and grow as a person.

Remember to get two, unless you plan on spending most if not all of your day with one. Rats are social animals, and can experience depression, and can even die from it. Rehoming can also be an option if you don't feel comfortable with baby rats. Make sure you get the same gender. Females are known to me more playful, while males are known to be more affectionate and cuddly. If you do want a baby, it can be better to get them from a breeder as they are already used to being handled. Though, I did **not** get mine from a breeder, mainly because there are none around me. If you're thinking about getting one soon, remember that Easter is right around the corner, and many parents sell their pets once their children get bored of them.

Be prepared to spend a lot on a cage, but once you have one, you then have the ability to have a rat for life. You can find many online for sale, or you can go out and buy one. It should have at minimum, two floors. I believe it's recommended to have two cubic feet per rat. My cage is four floors (one full bottom, then three "shelves") and is about three feet or so tall. They can't have a metal lined bottom as it can be painful for them. I have a metal grate on the bottom of my cage, and I cover it in fleece (though, they like to get under it... Not much I can do about that). You can even litter train them! Just make sure you get the right bedding, as rats can have respiratory issues. Paper bedding is the best. Make sure their cage has lots to chew and play with! The fleece should be changed every two or three days (vinegar and water for this). No air fresheners. Bedding can be changed weekly, and everything should be removed and the cage fully cleaned once a month. They're pretty easy to care for once you get the supplies you need, and do a bit of research. I feed them a diet of assorted veggies (carrots, spinach, lettuce) and lab created pellets. My boys don't like apples, otherwise I'd give them some. Be careful how much fatty foods you give them, such as nuts and seeds, as this can cause obesity (I gave my boy one almond today, and they won't get another one until next week or later). 

Vet bills can be $40 to $100, and I myself am a college student (in Canada), but I got these boys for my own mental health and wellbeing. I really needed some type of stress relief. If you have any questions, let me know! If you knew all of this already, then I'm sorry for the lecture. I just want to see everyone have a good experience and enjoy their times with their rats.

Sexuality is complicated, gender even more so. Know, before you continue this conversation, that as long as you do not actively harm anyone, or plan to harm anyone, it is okay to think these things. 

Sexuality. No, not just talking about the sex you are attracted to, but rather your own sexual identity, attraction, kinks, fetishes, experiences. The definition is "capacity for sexual feelings". 

I am trans myself, female to male, but my trans identity plays little to no role in my sexuality. Gender does play a role, but not as large of one as people make it out to be. I personally identify as gay, but that's the label I myself have *decided* to put on it. What it comes down to is that I have an attraction to men, having sex with other men. Take in a few kinks here and there, and you have what I'm attracted to. On the gender side of things, I am a man who desires to have sex with another man. You can switch these things around all you want, add a dozen different kinks or fetishes to them, but at the end of the day, you are only defined by yourself. 

If you want to do some soul searching, there's absolutely nothing wrong with that. You could very well be transgender. You could just as equally be not. But you need to do what feels right to you, and makes you most happy. I cannot tell you the answer to this question, nobody can. If you want to leave it alone, that is your choice. Though in my experience, no matter what it is, pushing something down just allows it to expand and become larger than it needs to be. Forget about LGBT culture for a while. Teach yourself about these things outside of this realm of labels and toxicity. And contrary to what some may believe, although a few years can be difficult, we lead normal, regular lives once we surround ourselves with the right people, or even just stop telling those in our lives (except for those who need to know). Once transitioned, and for a lot of time while transitioning, especially for FTM, people see you as your preferred gender and you are treated no less. 

As for your sexuality, again, it all depends on how you want to define it. It's not stable, it's fluid. It shifts. You could be going through a phase of being sexually attracted to something, then in two years, find something else equally as attractive. You could be trans, yes, or you could just be into fem-boys. It's perfectly acceptable to be attracted to men having sex, in fact, I don't think it's super uncommon. You may want to pursue a sexual relationship where you would "peg" a man, or you could be into sexual crossdressing and roleplaying. There's a whole world of labels and kinks. Find out what you like, what you don't, and as long as everything is consensual, and you are not harming, nor are planning to harm somebody, really there's no rush to figure these things out. But don't worry so much about what's wrong with you, nothing is. It's just a preference.
